chapter_title: Digital Input: Reading Buttons and Switches

screens.title: Digital Input: Reading Buttons and Switches
screens.subtitle: How to read switches reliably with pull resistors and debouncing

narration.text: In this short module you will learn how an Arduino reads a button or switch, why an unconnected pin can produce noisy, unpredictable readings, and practical techniques to make readings stable. Reading a digital input starts with telling the microcontroller which pin you will use and then asking for its state. But that alone is not enough. If the pin is left floating it will pick up electrical noise and flip randomly. We prevent that with pull-up or pull-down resistors. You will learn both external resistor wiring patterns and the convenient internal pull-up the Arduino provides. We also cover switch bounce—what causes a single mechanical press to look like many presses—and a simple software debouncing pattern that uses non-blocking timing with the board clock. By the end, you will be able to wire a button, enable INPUT_PULLUP, and write a sketch that toggles an LED reliably. Think about why a stable signal matters: it avoids false triggers and supports responsive, predictable interfaces.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Use pull resistors and debounce logic so digital reads are stable and reliable.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These learning objectives focus on concrete skills you will practice. First, you will configure an Arduino pin as an input and read its state using the standard input A P I. That skill lets your sketch detect whether a switch or button is active. Second, you will understand floating inputs: what happens when a pin is left not connected and why electrical noise makes those readings unreliable. Third, you will learn to use pull-up or pull-down resistors, including the Arduino's internal pull-up option, so you can wire buttons without extra components in many cases. Finally, you will implement software debouncing with a non-blocking timing approach. That debounce pattern prevents a single mechanical press from registering multiple events. Each objective is a stepping-stone: configure the pin, ensure it has a stable reference, choose the correct pull strategy, and handle bounce in code. Together these skills let you create reliable button-driven interactions such as toggling an LED or navigating a menu.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Assessment
screens.subtitle: How to practice these skills and what mastery looks like

narration.text: Now that you know the objectives, this view explains how to practice and verify them. To master configuring inputs, wire a pushbutton to any digital pin and write a sketch that reads it repeatedly and reports HIGH or LOW. To check your understanding of floating inputs, temporarily leave a pin unconnected and observe how the reading behaves; that noisy reading shows why a pull resistor is required. For pull resistors, build both a pull-down and a pull-up circuit so you can compare which state is default and how wiring changes the logic level when pressed. To verify software debouncing, implement the millis-based debounce and toggle an LED on each stable press. Mastery means your LED toggles once per human press even if the switch bounces. An assessment question you should be able to answer is why enabling INPUT_PULLUP makes the unpressed button read HIGH and what would happen if you used plain INPUT with no resistor.

screens.title: What is a digital input?
screens.subtitle: How an Arduino interprets HIGH and LOW signals

narration.text: A digital input is a pin that can be read as either HIGH or LOW, representing a binary signal. When you configure a pin as an input, the microcontroller places that pin in a high-impedance state so it can sense voltage without driving it. This lets external components like switches, sensors, or buttons determine the pin voltage. A basic sequence is to call the configuration function to declare the pin an input, then repeatedly sample its state in the main loop to take action when a change is detected. For example, reading a button connected to 5 volts yields a HIGH value when the button provides voltage and LOW when tied to ground. A common misconception is that configuring a pin as input is enough to guarantee a stable reading; it is not. The pin must also have a defined reference when no external source is driving it. We'll show wiring examples and an annotated code panel so you can see how configuration and reads work together. Think about why the microcontroller does not drive the pin: that avoids fighting external components and preserves the correct sensed voltage. How would your sketch react if the pin flipped for no reason? That question leads directly to pull resistors.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A digital input senses HIGH or LOW without driving the pin; stable readings require a defined reference.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › What is a digital input?
Concept and code
An input is high-impedance so it senses voltage. You configure it once and read inside loop().
// Configure pin 2 as input
pinMode(2, INPUT);

// Later, in loop:
int buttonState = digitalRead(2);
Example
A button connects pin 2 to 5V when pressed; reading that pin returns HIGH during press.
Explanation bullets
  • Inputs do not source or sink significant current; they measure voltage.
  • A pin must have a defined voltage otherwise readings may be unreliable.
  • digitalRead returns discrete HIGH or LOW values representing voltage thresholds.
  • Use pinMode to set the pin before you attempt to read it.
Key takeaway
Always define a default reference for inputs to avoid random readings.
Common misconception
Assuming pinMode alone ensures stable readings; you still need a pull resistor if nothing else drives the pin.

screens.title: Floating Inputs vs. Defined Inputs
screens.subtitle: Why an unconnected pin produces noise and how to fix it

narration.text: A floating input happens when a digital pin is not connected to a stable voltage source. In that state the pin is high impedance and can pick up stray electromagnetic noise from the surroundings, which leads to random HIGH and LOW readings. This unpredictability is the core problem you must solve. The fix is simple in principle: provide a default path to either 5 volts or ground through a resistor so the pin sits at a known state when the switch is open. A pull-down ties the pin to ground using a resistor so the unpressed state reads LOW. A pull-up ties the pin to the positive rail so the unpressed state reads HIGH. Compare the two patterns: pull-down wiring requires an external resistor, while pull-up wiring can use the Arduino internal pull-up resistor in many cases. A common mistake is using a very low value resistor which will waste current or interfere with the button press. Use around 10 kiloohms in passive external circuits. Practice by leaving a pin floating and then adding a pull to observe the difference. Which default state feels more natural depends on your wiring and logic preferences.

keyIdea.title: Fix floating inputs
keyIdea.text: Pull resistors provide a default voltage so an input has a stable reading when the button is not pressed.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Floating vs Defined
Floating input
Without a resistor the pin has no reference and can randomly read as HIGH or LOW. This creates false triggers.
Symptom
Unstable readings, spurious button events, erratic behavior.
Test
Leave the pin unconnected and observe logged values; they will fluctuate.
Defined input with pull resistor
Attach a 10kΩ resistor to ground or 5V so the pin defaults to a known state when the switch is open.
Symptom
Stable readings; button press reliably produces a single change.
Best practice
Use ~10kΩ for external pull resistors. Reserve very low values to avoid current waste.
Example wiring notes
Pull-down: resistor between pin and ground; button connects pin to 5V when pressed. Pull-up: resistor between pin and 5V; button connects pin to ground when pressed.

screens.title: Pull-down vs Pull-up Resistors
screens.subtitle: How wiring determines default logic state and wiring choices

narration.text: Pull-down and pull-up resistors establish the default logic level of a pin when the button is open. A pull-down resistor ties the pin toward ground through a resistance, so the unpressed state reads LOW; pressing the button connects the pin to 5 volts and produces HIGH. Many hobby tutorials show this pattern because it reads intuitively: pressed equals HIGH. The alternative is a pull-up resistor which ties the pin toward 5 volts, so the unpressed state reads HIGH and pressing the button pulls the pin to ground producing LOW. On Arduino boards you can often avoid an external pull-up resistor by enabling the internal pull-up in software. When you use internal pull-up, remember the logic is inverted: a pressed button reads LOW. Wiring choice affects your code because you must interpret which state indicates a press. A common mistake is forgetting to add any pull resistor; the result is a floating pin. Another is using the wrong pull orientation in code and misreading the button state. Try both patterns and observe which suits your circuit best. Pull-down vs Pull-up Resistors means pull-down gives unpressed low, pull-up yields unpressed high; using internal pull-up inverts pressed logic.. In practical terms, how wiring determines default logic state and wiring choices. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pull orientation matters
keyIdea.text: Pull-down gives unpressed LOW, pull-up yields unpressed HIGH; using internal pull-up inverts pressed logic.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Pull-down vs Pull-up
Pull-down (external resistor)
Resistor from pin to ground. Unpressed state reads LOW. Press connects pin to 5V and reads HIGH.
Wiring
Pin → resistor → ground. Button connects pin to 5V when pressed.
Note
Requires external resistor; common in circuits where you prefer pressed=HIGH logic.
Pull-up (external or internal)
Resistor from pin to 5V. Unpressed reads HIGH. Press connects pin to ground and reads LOW.
Wiring
Pin → resistor → 5V. Button connects pin to ground when pressed. Internal pull-up avoids external resistor.
Note
When using INPUT_PULLUP, code must treat LOW as the active pressed state.
Quick test
Try both and log values. Confirm whether pressed yields HIGH or LOW and adjust your condition checks accordingly.

screens.title: Internal Pull-up Resistors on Arduino
screens.subtitle: Enable INPUT_PULLUP and understand inverted logic

narration.text: Many Arduino boards offer an internal pull-up resistor that you can enable in software. By setting the pin mode to the internal pull-up variant, the microcontroller connects a weak resistor from the pin to the positive rail so the pin reads HIGH by default. This saves you from placing an external resistor on the breadboard. To use it in practice, wire the button so that pressing it connects the pin to ground. Then the pressed state reads LOW because the button overcomes the weak pull-up and pulls the pin to ground. A common point of confusion is that enabling the internal pull-up flips the logical sense of the button compared with a pull-down wiring. If your code expects HIGH on press, you must invert the check when using INPUT_PULLUP. Another pitfall is forgetting the wiring: if you wire the switch to 5V instead of ground when using input pull-up, you'll short 5V to 5V through the switch when pressed. Always connect the switch to ground when using the internal pull-up. Internal Pull-up Resistors on Arduino means use input_pullup to avoid an external resistor. remember pressed will read low.. In practical terms, enable input_pullup and understand inverted logic. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: INPUT_PULLUP
keyIdea.text: Use INPUT_PULLUP to avoid an external resistor. Remember pressed will read LOW.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Internal Pull-up
Enable the internal pull-up
pinMode(2, INPUT_PULLUP);
With this setting the pin reads HIGH when the button is open, and reads LOW when the button connects the pin to ground.
Example wiring
Connect one side of the button to the digital pin and the other side to ground. No external resistor needed.
Why use internal pull-up
  • Reduces parts; convenient for simple button inputs.
  • Prevents floating without extra components.
  • Requires you to invert logic in code because pressed equals LOW.
Common mistake
Connecting the button to 5V instead of ground while using INPUT_PULLUP creates a direct short when pressed. Always wire to ground.

screens.title: Switch Bounce: Why a single press can register many
screens.subtitle: Mechanical contacts and the need for debouncing

narration.text: When you press a mechanical switch its metal contacts do not close and remain closed instantly. Instead they vibrate and make intermittent contact for a few milliseconds. That vibration causes the electrical connection to rapidly open and close multiple times. If your code samples the pin during that period and acts on every change, you will count many presses when the user performed only one. This is known as switch bounce. It is purely mechanical behavior and normal for most pushbuttons and switches. To handle it in software we add a short period of time after the first detected change where subsequent fluctuations are ignored. That interval is typically between 5 and 50 milliseconds depending on the hardware. The strategy reduces false events while still responding quickly to a human press. Practically, you capture the time of the first change using the board's clock and only accept the new state once the elapsed time exceeds a debounce threshold. This non-blocking approach keeps your program responsive to other tasks. keyIdea.title: Switch bounce
keyIdea.text: Mechanical contacts bounce for milliseconds; debounce using a short timed filter to accept only stable changes.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Switch Bounce
What happens on press
Contacts bounce for a few milliseconds, causing multiple transitions that look like multiple presses to fast code.
Symptoms
  • LED toggles multiple times from a single press.
  • Menu selections jump past expected items.
Practical tip
Use a short debounce window. Too short may still catch bounce; too long delays responsiveness.
Visual analogy
Imagine a bouncing rubber ball: each contact is a brief event. Debounce waits until the bouncing stops before counting one hit.
Debounce interval
Typical 5–50 ms. Use 50 ms for noisy switches, shorter for faster UI.
Non-blocking vs blocking
Non-blocking uses millis() so other tasks run. Blocking with delay() stops the CPU and should be avoided for interactive systems.

screens.title: Debounce with millis(): Pattern and rationale
screens.subtitle: How the non-blocking debounce code works, step by step

narration.text: This screen walks through a common non-blocking debounce pattern that uses the board clock instead of pause calls. The pattern tracks three pieces of state: the last observed raw reading from the pin, the last time a change was detected, and the debounced stable button state. When a new raw reading differs from the previously observed raw reading, the code updates the timestamp of that change. The code then checks whether the elapsed time since that timestamp exceeds a debounceDelay. Only after the reading remains stable for that whole interval do we commit the new state and trigger any press logic. This avoids counting transient fluctuations. Using millis() rather than delay() keeps the main loop able to perform other tasks concurrently. Expect to see variables holding times in milliseconds, a constant debounceDelay like fifty, and a comparison that assigns the stable state when the time threshold is passed. Common mistakes are resetting the timer incorrectly or using delay() which blocks. The pattern is simple but effective for most pushbuttons. Debounce with millis(): Pattern and rationale means track the last raw reading and the last change time; accept a state only after it remains stable for the debounce interval.. In practical terms, how the non-blocking debounce code works, step by step. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Debounce pattern
keyIdea.text: Track the last raw reading and the last change time; accept a state only after it remains stable for the debounce interval.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Debounce with millis()
Key variables in the pattern
  • lastDebounceTime: timestamp of the last raw change.
  • debounceDelay: threshold in milliseconds to wait before accepting new state.
  • lastButtonState and buttonState: track raw and stable states.
Code excerpt
unsigned long lastDebounceTime = 0;
const unsigned long debounceDelay = 50;
int lastButtonState = HIGH;
int buttonState = HIGH;

void loop() {
  int reading = digitalRead(2);
  if (reading != lastButtonState) {
    lastDebounceTime = millis();
  }
  if ((millis() - lastDebounceTime) > debounceDelay) {
    if (reading != buttonState) {
      buttonState = reading;
      if (buttonState == LOW) {
        // button pressed
      }
    }
  }
  lastButtonState = reading;
}
Explanation cards
Why store lastButtonState?
It lets you detect a raw transition so you can start the debounce timer when the input first changes.
Why compare elapsed time?
Comparing millis() to the saved timestamp ensures the reading is stable for the full debounce window before you act.
Key takeaway
This pattern filters transient changes while keeping the loop free for other work.

screens.title: Line-by-line: How the debounce logic flows
screens.subtitle: Walk through the control flow and state updates in the debounce example

narration.text: Let's step through the debounce loop to see how control flows and where you should place your response logic. The loop starts by sampling the pin to get the current raw reading. If this reading differs from the previously observed raw reading, we record the current time as the lastDebounceTime. This marks the beginning of a potential state change. We then check whether the difference between the current time and lastDebounceTime exceeds the debounceDelay. If it does, the reading has remained unchanged for the full interval; we then compare it to the stored stable buttonState. If the stable state differs from the reading, we accept the new stable state and trigger whatever action you need, for example toggling an LED. Finally, we update lastButtonState to the latest raw reading so the next loop iteration can detect a new transition. This order is important: resetting the timer when the raw changes, waiting the full debounce window, then accepting only stable changes avoids false triggers. A common error is updating lastButtonState too early or using delay(), which blocks and prevents other tasks from running.

keyIdea.title: Control flow
keyIdea.text: Detect raw change, timestamp it, wait for stability, then commit the new state and run response logic.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Debounce Flow
Step-by-step flow
  1. Read the pin to get the current raw value.
  2. If raw differs from last raw, store the current time as the change timestamp.
  3. If the time since that timestamp exceeds debounceDelay, consider the reading stable.
  4. If this stable reading differs from stored stable state, update stable state and run the response.
  5. Always update last raw reading for the next iteration.
Where to put actions
Place button-pressed actions inside the branch that commits the new stable state so they run once per real press.
Common mistakes and fixes
Using delay()
Blocks the loop and prevents other tasks. Replace with millis()-based timing for non-blocking behavior.
Resetting timer incorrectly
Only reset the timer when raw reading changes. Resetting elsewhere prevents the window from closing.
Key takeaway
Correct placement of the timing check guarantees one action per physical press.

screens.title: Build: Toggle LED with INPUT_PULLUP and Debounce
screens.subtitle: A guided lab to connect a button and toggle the onboard LED reliably

narration.text: This hands-on activity ties wiring and code together. Use pin 2 for the button and pin 13 for the LED. Enable the internal pull-up on the button pin so you need no external resistor. Wire the button so one side goes to pin 2 and the other side goes to ground. In code set pinMode for the LED as an output and for the button as input with pull-up. In loop read the button and use the millis()-based debounce pattern to detect stable presses. On each confirmed press toggle the LED state and write it to the output pin. Testing helps: watch the LED while pressing slowly and rapidly. If the LED toggles more than once per physical press, increase the debounce delay. If the LED feels sluggish, lower the delay slightly. This lab reinforces how wiring choices influence logic levels and how debounce makes the action predictable. When you finish, answer why a pressed button reads LOW in this setup and what would happen if you omitted the pull-up. Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Toggle LED Lab
Wiring checklist
  • Button: one side to digital pin 2, other side to ground.
  • LED: longer leg to pin 13, shorter leg to ground (with current-limiting resistor if external LED).

If the LED never toggles, verify the button is wired to ground and the pin mode uses pull-up.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Pro Tips
screens.subtitle: Avoid wiring and code mistakes that lead to unreliable inputs

narration.text: As you build button-driven interfaces you'll repeatedly encounter a few common pitfalls. First, forgetting a pull resistor leaves the pin floating; the symptom is random state changes. Fix: add a pull-up or pull-down. Second, using delay() for debounce blocks the loop and prevents other important tasks—replace it with the millis() pattern so the system remains responsive. Third, miswiring when using INPUT_PULLUP can short the rail if you connect the switch to 5V instead of ground. Always wire the button to ground when the internal pull-up is enabled. Fourth, choosing an inappropriate debounce interval either fails to remove bounce or makes the system feel sluggish. Start at fifty milliseconds and adjust. Pro tips: use INPUT_PULLUP for quick prototypes to save parts, log raw readings to the serial line when debugging, and keep button handling logic focused—toggle or queue actions on stable events so your main loop stays clean. These practices make UIs predictable and robust. Common Mistakes and Pro Tips means use millis()-based debounce, correct wiring for input_pullup, and a sensible debounce interval like 50 ms.. In practical terms, avoid wiring and code mistakes that lead to unreliable inputs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Avoid these errors
keyIdea.text: Use millis()-based debounce, correct wiring for INPUT_PULLUP, and a sensible debounce interval like 50 ms.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Mistakes & Tips
Common mistakes
  • Leaving the pin as plain INPUT with no resistor causes floating readings.
  • Using delay()-based debounce stops other processing and reduces responsiveness.
  • Wiring the switch to 5V while using INPUT_PULLUP creates a short when pressed.
  • Using too short a debounce window that still lets bounce through.
Pro tips
Enable INPUT_PULLUP for quick builds and minimal components, but invert logic in code.
Log raw readings to observe bounce before tuning debounceDelay.
Handle actions on debounced transitions so your code responds once per press.
Why it matters
Correct handling prevents false triggers and enables reliable human interaction with your device.

narration.text: Here are the three critical ideas to keep in mind. First, digital inputs must have a defined reference; without a pull resistor the pin floats and readings become unreliable. Second, pull-up and pull-down resistors set the default logic level. The Arduino internal pull-up is handy and removes the need for an external resistor, but it inverts the pressed logic so pressed reads as low. Third, mechanical switches bounce for milliseconds. Use a millis()-based debounce pattern that timestamps raw changes and only accepts a new state after it remains stable for the debounce interval. These three concepts—defined reference, pull orientation, and debounce—work together to make button-driven systems predictable and user friendly. When you wire and code with these ideas, your interfaces become robust to electrical noise and mechanical quirks. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Remember
keyIdea.text: Defined default states and debounce are essential to reliable digital input handling.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Key Concepts
Defined reference
A pull resistor prevents floating and establishes stable HIGH or LOW when the button is open.
Pull-up vs pull-down
Pull-down defaults to LOW; pull-up defaults to HIGH. INPUT_PULLUP inverts pressed logic.
Debounce with millis()
Use timing to accept a state only after it has been stable for the debounce window to avoid false triggers.
Summary takeaway

Combine clear wiring and a simple debounce pattern to make button inputs predictable and robust in your projects.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three one-line reminders for quick recall

narration.text: Keep these three reminders handy while you build. First, always ensure a defined default: use a pull resistor or INPUT_PULLUP so the pin is never floating. Second, remember that INPUT_PULLUP inverts the logic: unpressed reads HIGH and pressed reads LOW, so adapt your condition checks. Third, debounce mechanically noisy switches with a short millis()-based window to accept only stable transitions. These short rules will help you avoid the most common problems and let your button-driven interfaces behave consistently. When coding and wiring, ask yourself: is the pin defined, is the wiring matching the code's logic, and am I filtering bounce without blocking the loop? What to Remember means defined default, inverted logic with input_pullup, and millis()-based debounce.. In practical terms, three one-line reminders for quick recall. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Quick Reference
Default defined
Use a pull resistor or INPUT_PULLUP so the pin has a known state when open.
INPUT_PULLUP
Internal pull-up saves parts; pressed reads LOW, so invert logic in code.
Debounce
Use millis() timing threshold to accept only stable changes and avoid delay().
Final tip
When debugging, log raw values to the serial monitor to see bounce and confirm your debounce window.
